procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejecting the appeals in limine for being presented out of time.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: On a reference under s. 66(1) of the Act, the Punjab High Court held that the orders of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner were made under s. 30(2) and were not appealable under s. 33 of the Act.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Certificate to appeal to this Court against this order having been refused by the High Court, the appellant applied for and obtained leave to appeal to this Court under article 136 of the Constitution, and that is how the appeal comes before us.

issue.issue_text: Whether an appeal presented out of time is still considered an appeal, and whether an order dismissing it as time-barred is an order passed in an appeal.

facts: An assessee filed an appeal against an assessment order, but the appeal was presented after the statutory time limit had expired.
The Appellate Assistant Commissioner refused to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal as being time-barred.

The question before the Supreme Court was whether this dismissal order was passed under Section 31 of the Act, which would make it appealable, or under a different section (like Section 30(2)), which would not allow for a further appeal.
law: Section 30 of the relevant Act confers a substantive right of appeal on an assessee.
Section 31 is the only provision in the Act that governs the hearing and disposal of appeals.
Section 33 allows for a further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against any order passed under Section 31.
application: The Court first established that an appeal presented out of time is still considered an appeal in the eyes of the law. It rejected the view that an appeal filed late is not an appeal at all unless the delay is formally condoned.
Following this principle, the Court reasoned that if a late appeal is still an appeal, then any order disposing of it must be an order passed 'in appeal'.
The Court then determined that since Section 31 is the sole provision dealing with the disposal of appeals, an order dismissing an appeal as time-barred must necessarily fall under Section 31.

The Court addressed the counter-argument that an order under Section 31 must decide the case on its merits (i.e., confirm, reduce, or enhance the assessment). It held that this is not necessary. An order that dismisses an appeal on a preliminary point, such as limitation, has the *effect* of confirming the original assessment, which is sufficient to bring it within the scope of Section 31.

Finally, the Court explicitly rejected the distinction made by some High Courts between dismissing an appeal before or after it is formally admitted. It held that it makes no difference; in either case, the dismissal order is one passed under Section 31.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an appeal presented out of time is still an appeal, and an order dismissing it as time-barred is an order passed in appeal under Section 31. Therefore, such an order is appealable under Section 33.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation is an order made under section 31 of the Income-tax Act.

law.fact: An appeal presented out of time is still legally considered an appeal, and an order dismissing it as time-barred is an order passed 'in appeal'.
text_evidence: An appeal presented out of time is 1m appeal and an order dis- missing it as time-barred is one passed in appeal.

law.fact: Section 31 of the Income-tax Act is the only provision that deals with the hearing and disposal of appeals.
text_evidence: Section 31 is the only provision relating· to the hearing and dis· posal of appeals and if an order dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation as in the present case is one passed in appeal it must fall within s. 31...

law.fact: For an order to fall under section 31, it is not necessary for it to decide the case on its merits. It is sufficient if the effect of the order is to confirm the original assessment.
text_evidence: To fall within s. 31 it is not necessary that the order should expressly address itself to and decide on the merits of the assessment and it is sufficient that the effect of the order is to confirm the assess- ment as when the appeal is dismissed on a preliminary point.

application.fact: The Court reasoned that since an appeal filed late is still an appeal, any order disposing of it must fall under the only section governing the disposal of appeals, which is section 31.
text_evidence: On the principles laid down in these decisions, it must be held that an appeal pre- sented out of time is an appeal, and an order dismiss- ing it as time-barred is one passed in appeal.

Then, the next question is whether it is an order passed under section 31 of the Act. That section is the only provision relating to the hearing and dis- posal of appeals, and if an order dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation is one passed in appeal, it must fall within section 31.

application.fact: The Court rejected the argument that a dismissal on limitation grounds is not covered by section 31 because it doesn't address the merits of the assessment. It held that the practical effect of such a dismissal is the confirmation of the original assessment, which is an outcome contemplated by section 31.
text_evidence: .... although the Appellate Assistant Commis- sioner did not hear the appeal on merits and held that the appeal was barred by limitation his order was under section 31 and the effect of that order was to confirm the assessment which had been made by the Income-tax Officer".

application.fact: The Court explicitly resolved a conflict among lower courts by stating that it makes no difference whether the appeal was dismissed for being time-barred before or after it was formally admitted.
text_evidence: Held therefore that the orders of the Appellate Assistant Com- missioner holding that there were no sufficient reasons for excusing the delay and rejecting the appeals as time-barred would be orders passed under s. 31 and would be open to appeal, and it would make no difference in the position whether the orders of dismissal were made before or after the appeals were admitted.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an order from the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation is an order made under section 31 of the Income-tax Act. The Court reasoned that such a dismissal is an order passed 'in appeal,' and its effect is to confirm the original assessment, thereby falling within the scope of section 31, regardless of whether the merits were considered or whether the dismissal occurred before or after the appeal was admitted. Consequently, such an order is appealable.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order dismissing an appeal as time-barred under section 31 is appealable under section 33 of the Income-tax Act.

facts: An assessee (the appellant) filed appeals against tax assessments after the prescribed time limit had expired.
The Appellate Assistant Commissioner was asked to condone the delay but refused and dismissed the appeals as time-barred.
The assessee then appealed this dismissal to the Appellate Tribunal.

The Tribunal dismissed this second appeal, reasoning that the Commissioner's order was made under section 30(2) (refusing to condone delay) and not section 31 (disposing of an appeal), and therefore, no further appeal was allowed under section 33.
law: Section 30 of the Income-tax Act provides the right of appeal and the time limits for filing it, including a provision (s. 30(2)) for the Appellate Assistant Commissioner to condone delays.
Section 31 is the only provision that governs the hearing and disposal of appeals. It specifies that the Commissioner can confirm, reduce, enhance, or annul the assessment.
Section 33 grants a right of further appeal to the Appellate Tribunal against any order passed under section 31.
application: The Supreme Court first addressed whether an appeal filed out of time is legally considered an "appeal". It concluded that "An appeal presented out of time is an appeal and an order dismissing it as time-barred is one passed in appeal."
The Court then reasoned that since section 31 is the only provision in the Act for the "hearing and disposal of appeals," any order that disposes of an appeal must fall under this section.

It rejected the argument that an order must decide the case on its merits to be considered an order under section 31. The Court held that an order dismissing an appeal on a preliminary ground, such as being time-barred, has the *effect* of confirming the original assessment. This brings it within the scope of section 31.

The Court explicitly stated that it makes "no difference" whether the dismissal for being time-barred happens before or after the appeal is formally admitted for hearing. In either case, the resulting order is one of disposal under section 31.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that an order by an Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissing an appeal as time-barred is an order passed under section 31 of the Income-tax Act. Therefore, such an order is appealable to the Appellate Tribunal under section 33.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order, to fall under section 31, must decide the appeal on the merits of the assessment rather than on a preliminary issue like limitation.

facts: An appeal was presented to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner after the prescribed time limit.
The Appellate Assistant Commissioner refused to excuse the delay and dismissed the appeal as time-barred, without considering the merits of the assessment.
The central question was whether this dismissal order was passed under Section 31 of the Act, which would make it appealable under Section 33.
law: Section 30 of the Income Tax Act confers a right of appeal on the assessee.
Section 31 is the only provision that governs the hearing and disposal of appeals.
Section 33 provides for a further right of appeal against any order passed under Section 31.
application: The Court first established that an appeal presented out of time is still legally considered an "appeal," and an order dismissing it as time-barred is an "order passed in appeal."
Since Section 31 is the sole provision for the disposal of appeals, the Court reasoned that an order dismissing an appeal for being time-barred must fall within the scope of Section 31.
The Court rejected the counter-argument that an order under Section 31 must explicitly confirm, reduce, enhance, or annul the assessment, which would require a decision on the merits.

It held that it is not necessary for the order to expressly address the merits. Instead, it is sufficient that the *effect* of the order is to confirm the assessment. By dismissing the appeal on a preliminary point like limitation, the original assessment is left standing, which effectively confirms it.

The Court adopted a liberal construction, stating that Section 31 contemplates the overall "disposal or conclusion of the appeal," and the specific types of orders listed in the section are not exhaustive.
It concluded that the jurisdiction of the appellate authority is not limited to the merits of the assessment but also includes deciding preliminary issues like limitation.
This reasoning applies whether the dismissal for being time-barred occurs before or after the appeal is formally admitted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that an order must decide the merits of an assessment to fall under Section 31. It held that an order dismissing an appeal on a preliminary issue, such as being barred by limitation, is an order under Section 31 because its effect is to confirm the assessment and it disposes of the appeal. Therefore, such an order is appealable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an appeal presented out of time is still considered an appeal, and whether an order dismissing it as time-barred is an order passed in an appeal.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's action of appealing the dismissal to the Tribunal under section 33 implies their argument that an appeal, even if presented late, is still an appeal, and an order dismissing it is an order passed 'in an appeal' under section 31.
respondent_arguments: An appeal presented out of time is not a valid appeal to be disposed of under section 31. The respondent argued that an order dismissing such an appeal as time-barred was one under section 30(2), which deals with the admission of appeals, not a disposal of the appeal itself.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation is an order made under section 31 of the Income-tax Act.
appellant_arguments: An order dismissing an appeal for being time-barred is an order made under section 31 of the Act. The original dismissal orders were purported to be passed under section 31.
respondent_arguments: An order dismissing an appeal as time-barred is an order made under section 30(2) of the Act, not section 31. The respondent relied on an Allahabad High Court decision which held this view.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order dismissing an appeal as time-barred under section 31 is appealable under section 33 of the Income-tax Act.
appellant_arguments: An order dismissing an appeal as time-barred is appealable under section 33, which is why the appellant preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal.
respondent_arguments: Such an order is not appealable under section 33. The respondent's position, supported by the High Court and the Tribunal in this case, was that since the order was under section 30(2), no appeal lay against it under section 33.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order, to fall under section 31, must decide the appeal on the merits of the assessment rather than on a preliminary issue like limitation.
appellant_arguments: An order under section 31 does not have to be on the merits of the assessment. The jurisdiction of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner is not limited to the merits only and includes the power to decide on preliminary issues like limitation.
respondent_arguments: An order falls under section 31 only if it disposes of the appeal on its merits (e.g., confirming, reducing, or annulling the assessment). An order on a preliminary issue like limitation is not a disposal on the merits and therefore not an order under section 31.

cases.case_name: Nagendranath Dey v. Buresh Chandra Dey
cases.principle: An appeal presented out of time is still an appeal, and an order dismissing it as time-barred is one passed in an appeal.

cases.case_name: Special Manager of Court of Wards v. Commissioner of Income-tax
cases.principle: An order dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation was an order under section 31, and the effect of that order was to confirm the assessment.

cases.case_name: K. K. Porbunderwalla v. Commissioner of Income-tax
cases.principle: An order that disposes of or concludes an appeal, even on a preliminary ground like limitation, is an order under section 31 because the section contemplates a disposal or conclusion of the appeal, and the forms of orders specified in it are not exhaustive.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An application by a party to an appellate court, asking it to set aside or revise a decision of a subordinate court, is an appeal within the ordinary acceptation of the term, and it is no less an appeal because it is irregular or incompetent.
obiter: The legislature has evinced an intention to maintain the distinction well-recognised under the general law between what is a substantive right and what is a matter of procedural law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: An order from the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissing an appeal as barred by limitation is an order made under section 31 of the Income-tax Act, not section 30(2), and is therefore appealable to the Appellate Tribunal under section 33. The court reasoned that previous Supreme Court observations suggesting otherwise, specifically in *Commissioner of Income-tax, Madras v. Mtt. Ar. S. Ar. Arunachalam Chettiar*, were not a binding decision on this question because the point did not directly arise for decision in that case. An order dismissing an appeal on a preliminary ground like limitation is a final disposal that results in the affirmation of the order being appealed, and thus falls within the scope of section 31.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation to determine whether an order dismissing an appeal for being time-barred constitutes a disposal of the appeal under Section 31 or a refusal to admit the appeal under Section 30(2).
Application of the doctrine of precedent, distinguishing between a binding ruling and non-binding judicial observations (obiter dicta) to determine the precedential value of prior case law.
